db_evidence.notes: The episodes table (30sec granularity) fully and accurately covers the performance from ~213998/214011 s through 215348 s with detailed shot-by-shot text; a simple SQL range query over this window retrieves everything needed. However, the coarser event_chains table has a chain (event_chains:0000856, 'indoor arena performance viewing and ishowspeed's solo performance') whose end_s is arbitrarily capped at 214868 s -- roughly 8 minutes before the performance actually ends per the episodes text. Rollouts that keyed their answer off this chain boundary (rollout-01, rollout-04) undercounted; rollouts that stayed with the raw episodes rows or used clip_qa to visually confirm the true end (rollout-00, rollout-02, rollout-03) got durations close to or slightly above the reference.

root_causes: A stale/truncated event_chains summary row (end_s=214868) that undercuts the true performance duration; two of five rollouts trusted this coarse chain boundary over the more granular episodes evidence they had also retrieved, producing large undercounts (rollout-04 worst, at 14:30 vs ~20 min reference).

Ambiguity in what counts as 'watching the performance': the reference answer's own total_intervals exclude a ~96s stretch where the streamer performs himself rather than watches, but only rollout-01 attempted a similar subtraction; rollouts 00/03 included that stretch and modestly overshot (22:30 vs ~20 min).

Visual verification (clip_qa) targeted at the start/end transition points (rollout-02) resolved the true performance boundaries (214011-215348) more reliably than SQL-only or event_chain-only reasoning, and produced the top score.

Judge scoring shows some inconsistency: rollout-00 and rollout-03 submitted essentially the same duration and boundaries (22:30, 213998-215348) yet were scored 3 and 4 respectively; the only material difference is a garbled self-correction phrase in rollout-00's answer text.
what_worked: Running a wide-window SQL query over the 30sec-granularity episodes table (e.g. 213000-216500) reliably surfaces the true, continuous performance content, avoiding reliance on coarser/truncated event_chain summaries.

Using clip_qa specifically to visually confirm the start and end transition frames (rather than only the entry/seating moment) pinned down the correct boundaries and produced the best-scoring answer (rollout-02).

All 5 rollouts correctly located the general temporal region (~213998-215348s) and correctly identified this as the Shaolin stage-performance segment inside the main temple theater; none searched a wrong part of the timeline.
transferable_lessons: For duration questions, prefer the finest-granularity episodes rows over event_chains/event_steps summary boundaries -- chain-level start_s/end_s can be arbitrarily truncated mid-event and should be cross-checked against raw episode text before being used as a duration anchor.

When raw evidence (e.g. episodes rows) contradicts a coarser summary row (e.g. an event_chain's end_s) that was retrieved in the same session, prefer the raw evidence -- do not let a convenient summary override contradicting details already in context.

For 'how long did X watch Y' questions, explicitly consider whether periods where the subject is not passively watching (e.g. performing themselves) should be excluded, and state that assumption in the answer; this ambiguity is a real source of scoring variance independent of retrieval quality.

Use clip_qa to visually verify the precise start/end transition frames for duration questions rather than relying solely on text-summary boundaries -- it caught the true end of the performance (215348s) that two other rollouts missed via chain-based reasoning.
open_questions: Why the judge scored two near-identical answers (22:30 from the same 213998-215348 boundaries) as 3 vs 4 -- likely judge stochasticity/sensitivity to answer phrasing rather than a substantive difference in content.

Whether the reference answer's ~20-minute figure was itself derived by excluding the self-performance interlude, or is simply an imprecise 'about' estimate that happens to sit between the undercounting and overcounting rollouts.
